title: Long Day? Give Your Legs More Support
body: My husband laughed at me when I spent $25 on a pair of compression socks. Two weeks later, he asked me where his pair was. Let me explain. For 15 years, I’ve watched 12-hour shifts take a little more of my legs every year. Then a nurse I work with told me something I have never been able to forget. Swollen ankles are a warning light. Ignore them long enough and the heaviness stops going away overnight. Tight shoes, heavy legs, sock rings still there in the morning. Until the job quietly takes your evenings, your walks, the woman you used to be. Years before you’re ready. My old compression socks were doing half the job. They squeezed. That part worked. But they were so hot and itchy I rolled them down by lunch. Twelve hours on my feet, and my legs were fighting gravity with no help at all. Armadilo compression socks do both halves. 15 to 20 mmHg of firm, even compression around the ankle and calf. Bamboo-based yarn that breathes, hour after hour. A knit that’s still soft after 50 washes. A month later, I caught myself coming home light, easy, laughing like I used to. I did not get new socks. I got myself back. Do not let your legs decide when you stop. Armadilo. Buy two pairs, get two free. Don’t feel the difference? Every dollar back. He laughed at them. Now he steals mine for long drives.

title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear... Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start. Flexible arch support. Heel cushioning. A strengthening program. And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid. Right now, you can get four pairs for $30. So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them. School shoes. Sneakers. Cleats. Sports shoes. For me? That was a much easier decision than: Another specialist appointment. Another fitting. Another wait. Another $400 custom orthotic. title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear... Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start. Flexible arch support. Heel cushioning. A strengthening program. And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid. Right now, you can get four pairs for $30. So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them. School shoes. Sneakers. Cleats. Sports shoes. For me? That was a much easier decision than: Another specialist appointment. Another fitting. Another wait. Another $400 custom orthotic. And another argument with my kid about whether he'd actually wear it. Click below to see the Footstr InsoleX 👇

title: Every soccer-mom needs to see this ☝️
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. And I want to say this again because it's important: The custom orthotics did work when he wore them. That's not why I stopped using them. I stopped because the whole process was a nightmare. Appointments. Fittings. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. A rigid device my kid hated. And then... just when I finally convinced him to give them another chance... his feet were already too big. I did not want to start all over again. That's when Footstr's price stopped looking merely “cheap”... and started looking practical. Four pairs for $30. Instead of hundreds of dollars for one custom device. And four pairs meant I didn't have to move one insole around every day. One pair in his school shoes. One in his sneakers. One in his soccer cleats. One for another pair he wears regularly. That is a completely different decision from: “Do I want to spend another $400 and hope my kid actually wears them this time?” THEN I STARTED LOOKING AT WHY THEY FELT SO DIFFERENT I wanted to understand why he was keeping Footstr inside his shoes when he had fought the customs so hard. There were three things that made sense. 1 - FLEXIBLE ARCH SUPPORT Footstr isn't a completely flat foam pad. There is structure underneath the arch. When the foot starts rolling excessively inward, that support gives the arch something underneath it instead of simply following the collapse. But it still flexes with the foot. Walking. Running. Cutting. Playing. The goal isn't to lock his foot into one rigid shape. It's to give it a steadier base while he's moving. 2 - HEEL CUSHIONING Kids playing sports take an insane amount of repeated impact. Sprint. Stop. Jump. Land. Sprint again. Footstr combines the arch support with cushioning underneath the heel. So there's comfort where the foot lands... and structure where it needs support. 3 - THE STRENGTHENING EXERCISES This was the other big reason I liked them. I didn't want our long-term plan to be: “Put something in his shoe forever and hope.” The insole and the strengthening work have different jobs. The insole supports the arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet something to actually work on outside the shoe. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. That made much more sense to me. WHY I DON'T WANT TO GO BACK The pharmacy inserts? Easy to wear. Not enough structure for what I wanted. The custom orthotics? Plenty of structure. Expensive. Rigid. A whole specialist process. Quickly outgrown. And most importantly... my kid wouldn't consistently wear them. Footstr landed in the middle. More structure than the flat inserts we'd tried. More flexible than the customs he'd rejected. Cushioning under the heel. Support under the arch. Something he could actually keep inside his cleats while playing soccer. And inexpensive enough that keeping up with a growing kid didn't feel ridiculous. WHAT I WOULD EXPECT IF YOU JUST ORDERED First time they put them on: Don't expect fireworks. Honestly, the best answer might be: “They're comfortable.” Or: “They're fine.” That's a win. You don't want your kid thinking about the thing inside their shoe. First practice: This is the first real test. Cleats tightened. Feet getting hot. Running. Jumping. Cutting. See whether your kid actually keeps them in. That's what mattered most to me. First week: Watch the ordinary things. Are they still wearing them? Are you fighting about them before practice? Are they pulling them out halfway through? What do they say after the activities that normally bring on complaints? Over the next few weeks: Keep your expectations realistic. Footstr isn't going to magically rebuild a growing foot overnight. It's giving the arch and heel support during the activities that demand the most from them... while the strengthening exercises give you something proactive to work on as they grow. IF YOU JUST ORDERED... Don't panic like I did. When I clicked order that Tuesday night, I genuinely wondered whether I'd just bought another pair of insoles my kid would refuse to wear. A few weeks later... I was holding his $400 custom orthotics that he'd already outgrown... while Footstr was still sitting inside his soccer cleats. That comparison pretty much answered the question for me. IF YOU HAVEN'T ORDERED YET... If your kid's feet roll inward... Their feet, heels or knees complain after sports... Or you've already been through the nightmare of expensive custom orthotics they won't consistently wear... Footstr gives you a much simpler place to start. Flexible arch support. Heel cushioning. A strengthening program. And support designed around active, growing feet without locking them against something hard and rigid. Right now, you can get four pairs for $30. So instead of constantly moving one pair between shoes, you can keep them where your kid actually needs them. School shoes. Sneakers. Cleats. Sports shoes. For me? That was a much easier decision than: Another specialist appointment. Another fitting. Another wait. Another $400 custom orthotic. And another argument with my kid about whether he'd actually wear it. Click below to see the Footstr InsoleX 👇 https://getfootstr.com/products/footstr-insolex

title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. He had basically forgotten about them. TUESDAY — SECOND SOCCER PRACTICE This was the day I was really waiting for. Because almost anything new can survive one wear. The real question is: Will a kid keep wearing it after the novelty disappears? That's where we'd lost the custom orthotics. Again... they worked. When he wore them, his inward rolling looked better. But eventually he started pulling them out before practice. I'd argue. Then bargain. “Just wear them for half the session.” Then I'd find them in the bag anyway. So this time I said nothing. I didn't remind him about Footstr. I didn't ask whether he had put them in. I just watched. Full practice. Still inside his cleats. He came off the field sweaty. Hungry. Exhausted. But he hadn't removed his shoes halfway through practice. He hadn't complained about something hard digging into his foot. He hadn't handed me an insole. They just... stayed in. That sounds small. After everything we'd been through? It wasn't. WEEK 1 — THE FULL PICTURE Before Footstr: $400 custom orthotics. Specialist appointment. Assessment. Measurements. Fitting. Waiting for them to be made. Trying to convince my kid to actually wear them. Eventually finding them sitting in his soccer bag instead of underneath his feet. Then the cheap pharmacy inserts. Easy to wear. But almost completely flat. Gel heel pads. Comfortable... but not the structured support I was looking for. So it felt like there were two choices: Comfortable enough for my kid to wear... but barely any structure. Or: Enough structure... but so rigid he refused to keep them in. After one week with Footstr: He was wearing them. That was the first big difference. Sneakers. School shoes. Soccer cleats. I wasn't arguing with him before practice. I wasn't digging through the bottom of his bag afterward. And for the first time I felt like we'd found the middle ground we'd been missing. Soft enough that my kid would actually wear them. Structured enough to support his arch when his foot started rolling inward. And with cushioning underneath his heel for all the running, jumping and pounding his feet take during sports. WEEK 2 This was when I stopped thinking quite so much about the insoles... and started noticing everything around them. Normally after soccer I could tell how practice had gone before my son even said anything. The way he walked toward the car. How quickly he kicked his shoes off. Whether he started rubbing his knees. Nothing was suddenly perfect. He's still a nine-year-old playing soccer hard. He still gets tired. He still gets sore. But I wasn't seeing the same ritual after every single practice. And most importantly... the Footstrs were still in his shoes. Every day. That mattered. Because even the best support in the world can't help much when it's sitting at the bottom of a sports bag. WEEK 3 One night I noticed something strange. The ice pack was still in the freezer. Normally after a hard week of soccer, getting it out had almost become automatic. That week... I hadn't. Not because I'd made some decision to stop using it. I simply hadn't thought about it. Neither had my son. Again... nothing dramatic. No miracle. Just one little thing that used to be part of our routine... that suddenly wasn't happening as often. WEEK 4 — THEN I PULLED THE CUSTOM ORTHOTICS BACK OUT I got curious. Part of me still wondered whether we'd been stupid to abandon something we'd spent so much money on. So I asked my son: “Try your customs again.” He rolled his eyes. Eventually agreed. I put them into his shoes. He pushed his foot down... stopped... and immediately said: “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” At first I thought he just didn't want to wear them. Then I looked. His feet had grown. And that was the moment the economics of this whole thing really hit me. I'd spent around $400 on those orthotics. Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Getting them adjusted. Convincing him to wear them. Eventually giving up. Then finally getting him to try them again... only to realize he'd already outgrown them. So again I did the math. $400. Twice a year. $800 every year. My son is nine. He has a lot of growing left. By the time his feet stop changing, I could have spent thousands. title: Every soccer-mom needs to see this ☝️
body: WARNING: I made a huge mistake after buying Footstr insoles for my son. Don't do what I did. I almost threw them away. Three weeks after they arrived, I nearly pulled them out of his cleats and tossed them in the trash. Not because they weren't working. Because of what happened after he started wearing them. Let me explain. My son is 9, he plays soccer, and somewhere over the past year I had quietly accepted that sore feet were just part of who he was. The slow limp to the car after practice. The ankles rolling inward every time he stood barefoot. Me planning our weekends around how much his feet could handle. Our doctor looked at his flat feet, shrugged, and said he'd probably grow out of it. So I went down the internet rabbit hole. That's when I found Footstr. Insoles made for kids who overpronate, with flexible arch support, heel cushioning, and a foot strengthening program. Honestly, it seemed too simple. We had already spent $450 on custom orthotics. What was a kids' insole going to do that those couldn't? But the reviews from other soccer parents sounded exactly like my house. So I ordered. ===== MY FIRST MISTAKE I didn't tell my husband. Not because he wouldn't be supportive. I just didn't want to get his hopes up. Or mine. I pulled the old orthotic out of my son's cleat, slid the Footstr in, and handed him the shoe like it was nothing. By week two, something strange happened. He was still wearing them. That might sound small, but the $450 custom orthotics lasted about two weeks before I started finding them at the bottom of his soccer bag. He hated how hard they felt under his feet. The Footstrs just stayed in his shoes. School, practice, the park. I never had to argue once. And I noticed something else. He stopped kicking his shoes off the second he got in the car. ===== THE REAL PROBLEM STARTED IN WEEK THREE Saturday game. Normally I watch the second half differently than the other parents. I'm not watching the ball. I'm watching my son's run, waiting for it to turn into that heavy, flat-footed jog that means his feet are done. But this time? Nothing happened. He just... played. The whole game. Afterward he walked to the car talking about a goal he almost scored, and climbed in like a kid whose feet had never once been a topic in our family. That night after dinner, he asked my husband to go kick the ball around in the yard. I tensed up. Evenings were usually when his feet and legs were finished for the day. But before I could say "maybe tomorrow," he was already outside. ===== HERE'S WHERE I ALMOST MADE MY BIGGEST MISTAKE That next week, I caught myself watching him constantly. Waiting for the limp to come back. Waiting for him to wake up with sore legs again. Waiting for the other shoe to drop. And when it didn't, I did something ridiculous. I decided it couldn't be the insoles. I nearly took them out and put the custom orthotics back in. The expensive ones. The prescribed ones. The "real" ones. Because somewhere along the way, I'd been trained to believe that if a solution isn't expensive and complicated, it can't actually be doing anything. $450 and a specialist appointment felt serious. A comfortable insole my kid actually liked wearing felt too easy. I'm so glad I stopped myself. Because the customs never really had a chance to help him. They were so stiff and bulky inside his cleats that he wouldn't keep them on his feet. And support sitting at the bottom of a soccer bag isn't supporting anything. ===== WHAT I FINALLY LEARNED That was the week I sat down and actually researched what was going on with his feet. I found a study of 92,000 adolescents. The ones with moderate to severe flat feet had nearly double the rate of knee pain and low back pain compared to kids with normal arches. Another study from 2025 looked at school aged kids specifically. Children with flat feet scored 42 percent higher on a clinical pain scale than their classmates, and they were measurably less active because of it. Neither study proved that my son's feet were behind every complaint he ever had. But they explained something I'd been watching for a year without understanding it. When his arch rolled inward under his weight, his whole leg was working from a wobbly base. Every sprint, every cut, every landing started from a foot that collapsed a little with each step. Then I finally read what was actually behind the Footstr design. Structured arch support that flexes as he runs instead of locking his foot in place the way the customs did. It helps reduce that excessive inward rolling while he's wearing them. Heel cushioning, so all the pounding from running and jumping has a softer place to land. And the part I didn't appreciate when I ordered: the strengthening program. The insole and the exercises have two different jobs. The insole supports his arch and heel during the activities that put the most demand on his feet. The exercises give the muscles around his feet and arches something to work on outside the shoe as he grows. Support during activity. Strengthening work over time. This wasn't just a softer version of the orthotics. It was the first thing that felt like a plan instead of another thing we bought after he was already hurting. ===== THE SIDE EFFECT NOBODY WARNS YOU ABOUT About two months in, my husband said something on the drive home from a game that stuck with me. "He hasn't stopped talking since he got in the car." He was right. I hadn't realized how quiet those drives had gotten over the past year. How much of our family's energy went into managing his feet. The ice, the rest days, the bargaining over whether he could handle practice. I'm not going to tell you his feet became indestructible. He still gets tired. He still has sore days after a big tournament. But the sore days stopped running our week. ===== WHY MOST "SOLUTIONS" NEVER WORKED FOR US Before Footstr, we tried the whole list. Custom orthotics. To be fair, when he actually wore them, his ankles didn't roll inward as badly. But they were rigid, bulky inside his cleats, $450, and he'd outgrow them within the year. Support your kid refuses to wear isn't support. Pharmacy inserts. Soft, cheap, and completely flat. They just followed his foot down as the arch collapsed. Rest. His feet always felt better after a week off. And the complaints always came back once he was playing again. Better shoes. They helped a little. But the support stayed home every time he switched into his cleats. None of it dealt with what was happening underneath him. A foot rolling inward under his weight, step after step, all day long. ===== WHAT I WISH SOMEONE HAD TOLD ME SOONER If your kid's ankles roll inward when they stand. If their shoes wear down faster along the inside edge. If they limp after practice, ask to sit out, or say their feet are tired before they are. Please don't spend a year like I did, telling yourself it's just growing pains. And if you do try something and things start getting better, don't make my mistake. Don't talk yourself out of it just because it was simple. Right now Footstr is running their Back to School sale, and everything is 60% off. We paid $450 for orthotics that lived in a soccer bag. title: Don’t make the same mistake I did…
body: I ordered the Footstr InsoleX to fix my kid’s flat feet... And then I panicked. Was my kid going to even like these? What if he wore them once and pulled them straight back out of his cleats? What if this was just another pair of insoles that ended up sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag? I'd been through that before. Custom orthotics were the worst. And not because they didn't work. They actually did. When my son wore them, I could see that his feet weren't rolling inward nearly as much. The problem was everything it took just to get there. First we had to see a specialist. Then the assessment. Measurements. The fitting. Then we waited for them to be made. Then went back again to make sure everything fit properly. Hundreds of dollars later... we finally had these custom orthotics that were supposed to solve the problem. And my son hated wearing them. They were hard. Bulky inside his soccer cleats. He complained that they hurt his feet. At first I kept trying to convince him to give them another chance. “Just wear them for practice.” “Give them a few days.” “You'll get used to them.” Eventually I gave up. I started finding the $400 orthotics sitting in the bottom of his soccer bag instead of inside his shoes. All that money. All those appointments. All that waiting. And they weren't helping anyone sitting underneath a dirty jersey. Then a few months later, I finally convinced him to try them again. He pushed his foot into his shoe... stopped... and looked at me. “Mom, these don't fit anymore.” His feet had grown. Of course they had. He's a kid. I hadn't even really thought about that when we bought them. Then I learned that growing kids may need their orthotics replaced around every six months. So I did the math. $400 twice a year. $800 a year. And he still had years of growing left. By the time my son stopped growing, I could've spent thousands of dollars on custom orthotics. Thousands... on something I still had to argue with him to wear. And customs weren't the only thing we'd tried. Pharmacy insoles. Too flat. Barely any structure. Gel heel inserts. Soft, sure. But they didn't do much for the way his feet rolled inward when he ran. Heel cups. Different shoes. Stretching. Rest. We kept trying things. Some helped a little. Some did basically nothing. But eventually we always seemed to end up in the same place. His feet were still rolling inward when he played. His knees were still bothering him after harder practices. And I was still searching for another answer. So when I saw Footstr... I was interested. But I definitely wasn't convinced. The one thing that made ordering easier was the price. Compared with going through the custom-orthotic nightmare again... Specialist. Fitting. Waiting. Hundreds of dollars. Footstr felt like a pretty small gamble. Still... cheap doesn't matter if your kid won't wear them. So if you just ordered Footstr... Or you're about to order... Let me tell you exactly what happened. Day by day. So you know what to expect. THEY ARRIVED FRIDAY AFTERNOON The first thing I did was take them out of the package and bend them in my hands. They weren't what I expected. The top felt soft. The whole insole had some flex to it. But underneath the arch... there was actual structure. Not that flat piece of foam I'd gotten from pharmacy insoles. And not the rock-hard feeling of my son's custom orthotics either. I bent one again. Flexible. But not floppy. That immediately got my attention. Because that had basically been the problem with everything we'd tried. The comfortable stuff didn't give him enough support. The supportive stuff was so rigid he wouldn't wear it. Footstr looked like it might actually sit somewhere in the middle. But I'd spent enough money getting excited about things in my hands. The real test was getting them onto his feet. FRIDAY EVENING My son was sitting at the kitchen table when I brought over one of his cleats. I'd already taken his old insert out and slipped the Footstr inside. He looked at the shoe. Then at me. “What is it?” “Another insole.” He gave me the look. You know the one. So I told him: “Just try it. If you hate it, take it out.” He pushed his foot inside. Stood up. Walked across the kitchen. Stopped. Walked back. I was waiting for: “No.” Instead he looked down at his feet. Took another few steps. Then shrugged. “These are way softer.” Okay. Good start. But I wasn't celebrating. Walking around our kitchen for thirty seconds is very different from sprinting, cutting and stopping for an entire soccer practice. I'd been fooled by first impressions before. So I went to bed thinking: We'll see tomorrow. SATURDAY — DAY 1 Soccer practice. This was the first real test. Before he ran onto the field I told him: “If they bother you, take them out.” I didn't want him suffering through them because he knew I'd spent money. He nodded. Practice started. Twenty minutes. Still playing. Forty minutes. Still playing. Then the entire session. And I swear I spent half of practice watching his feet. Waiting for him to jog toward the sideline. Waiting for the cleat to come off. Waiting for him to pull the Footstr out and hand it to me. It never happened. He finished practice with them still inside his cleats. When he walked over, I immediately asked: “How were the insoles?” He shrugged. “Fine.” That was it. And weirdly... that was exactly the answer I wanted. I didn't want him obsessing over his insoles. I wanted him thinking about soccer. Still... one practice is one practice. SUNDAY — DAY 2 I put them into his regular sneakers. And then I waited. Normally my son notices everything I put inside his shoes. Too high. Too stiff. Feels weird. Shoe feels tight. This time? Nothing. We went through almost the entire day before I finally asked: “You still have those insoles in?” He looked confused for a second. Then remembered. “Oh. Yeah.” That got my attention. title: 400 Years Ago They Walked Without a Sound. Here's How.
body: Japanese lords built floors that chirped like birds the moment anyone stepped on them. Some are still in Kyoto today. They were built to catch one kind of man. The shinobi… Not because of the black outfits. Not because of the dark. Because of the way he walked, and what he walked in. Thin tabi, so he felt every floorboard. He landed on the front of his foot, then rolled down soft onto the heel. No noise, no wobble, and his own foot muscles did all the work. Then in the 1970s, shoe companies put thick foam under everything and called it comfort. You can't feel the ground, so you slam down on your heel every step. The muscles in your feet go quiet because the foam is doing their job. The bottoms burn 20 minutes into a walk. Calves lock up by evening. A little worse every year, no matter how good the shoes. Nothing's wrong with your feet. You changed shoes. Introducing SuperSocks WoodCarved 2.0. The one and only sock on the market with a patented sole, hand-sewn to your exact pressure points to reactivate your foot muscles. Foot biomechanists mapped where a bare foot presses the ground. Every wood-carved section is hand-sewn into that position on a five-toe sock, so: ✅ Your foot feels the ground again and lands the way a shinobi landed ✅ The muscle under each section fires every step, no foam doing its job ✅ Knees, hips and back stop taking the slam The first tabi were cut from a single piece of hide. These sections are full-grain cowhide, the top layer of the leather, so they hold up mile after mile. Dyneema® knit around them keeps rocks from cutting in. Give it two weeks. It starts in your feet, then the rest of you straightens up on top of them. 🔄 30-Day Money-Back Guarantee Walk the shinobi way and go wherever you want again.

title: Best Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis
body: If you've got plantar fasciitis, stop wearing shoes that fold in half. Soft and bendy feels comfortable in the shop... but it overloads your arch all day. Here are the 5 features I look for when helping patients recover: 1️⃣ Firm heel counter You want the back of the shoe to feel solid. This limits excessive pronation and keeps the ankle stable. 2️⃣ Deep, supportive heel cup It should wrap around your heel bone and spread pressure evenly. This reduces strain through the inside of the heel. @kurufootwear builds this directly into the shoe with their curved heel technology, so you can actually feel that medial heel support. 3️⃣ Higher heel to toe drop A thicker heel compared to the forefoot reduces strain on your calf, arch, and plantar fascia. 4️⃣ Stiffness through the midfoot If you can easily twist or fold the shoe, it is too soft. A firmer shoe gives your foot the stability it needs while healing. 5️⃣ Slight rocker This helps roll you forward so you are not overloading your big toe and arch with every step. The right shoe will not cure plantar fasciitis overnight... but the wrong shoe will slow your recovery down. Check out @kurufootwear's range of shoes. #ad

title: The 3 "Wide" Shoes I Tell Women to Skip
body: I make comfort shoes for women over 50. So you'd think I'd stay quiet about the competition. But I'm going to tell you the three "wide" shoes I'd never recommend, and why. They're all popular. They all say wide on the box. And women buy them by the thousands, then write to me that their toes are still crammed. Here's the problem. Almost every "wide" shoe is just a regular narrow shoe sized up. It gets longer, maybe a little roomier overall, but the front still tapers to a point, right where your toes are. That's not wide. That's narrow with extra length. A real wide shoe is shaped like an actual foot, wide and rounded where your toes sit, so they finally have room to spread. That's the one thing I built ours around. Have a look and see the difference for yourself.

Orthofeet happened and I genuinely don’t know why it took a decade. 12 hour standing days. walking, pivoting, crouching down to spot someone’s squat, back up, demoing more exercises. body: I used to think heel pain was just something I had to deal with. The worst part was always those first few steps after getting out of bed. I tried different shoes and insoles, but I still wanted something I could comfortably wear throughout the day. That’s when I tried Viasox Ankle Compression Socks. But what I really noticed was the cushioning. The triple-padded sole gave my heel an extra layer of softness with every step, while the 14 mmHg compression made my feet feel comfortably supported. I started wearing them during long days on my feet, while walking, traveling, and even just around the house. Now they’re one of those small things I reach for whenever I know I’m going to be on my feet all day. If plantar fasciitis has made standing and walking uncomfortable, give Viasox Ankle Compression Socks a try.

title: Relief for My Swollen, Aching Feet 👉
body: Every evening, my feet & ankles looked swollen and felt exhausted. I’d prop them up, loosen my shoes, and count the minutes until I could sit down. It didn’t matter if I had been walking all day or just running a few errands — by late afternoon, my ankles felt tight, heavy, and uncomfortable. My shoes felt snug. My legs felt tired. And I started planning my day around when I could finally get off my feet. I tried elevating them. I changed shoes. I even tried different socks. Nothing seemed to make a real difference. Honestly, I just wanted my feet to feel normal again. That’s when I came across Viasox Ankle Compression Socks. From the first wear, I could tell they weren’t like regular socks. The 14 mmHg compression feels supportive but not restrictive — snug enough to give your ankles that secure, held-in feeling without digging into your skin. They’re soft, breathable, and stay comfortably in place all day. After a few days I noticed my ankles didn’t feel as puffy by the evening. They felt more supported throughout the day, and I wasn’t constantly thinking about how uncomfortable my feet were. I could move around more freely without that heavy, tight sensation creeping in. It’s such a simple change, but it made a real difference in how I feel day to day. If you’re dealing with tired, swollen-feeling ankles by the end of the day, Viasox Ankle Compression Socks are absolutely worth trying. Sometimes the right support is all you need to feel like yourself again.
